quests.partialSentence: My manager said that she ____ the report by Friday.
quests.hint: In reported speech, 'will' usually changes to another form when reporting a past statement.
quests.explanation: When reporting a past statement, 'will' typically changes to 'would': 'said she would finish.'

quests.partialSentence: He told me that he ____ very tired after the long shift.
quests.hint: In reported speech, the present tense in the original statement usually shifts back one step.
quests.explanation: Reported speech generally shifts the present tense back to the past: 'is' becomes 'was.'

quests.partialSentence: They explained that they ____ already sent the invoice.
quests.hint: In reported speech, the present perfect usually shifts back to the past perfect.
quests.explanation: When reporting speech, the present perfect typically shifts to the past perfect: 'have' becomes 'had.'

quests.partialSentence: The agent said that our flight ____ delayed by two hours.
quests.hint: In reported speech, the present tense usually shifts back one step into the past.
quests.explanation: Reported speech shifts the present tense back: 'is delayed' becomes 'was delayed.'

quests.partialSentence: She mentioned that she ____ visit Japan the following year.
quests.hint: In reported speech, 'will' usually changes to another form.
quests.explanation: When reporting a statement, 'will' generally changes to 'would.'

quests.partialSentence: He said that he ____ never been to that country before.
quests.hint: When reporting speech, present perfect verbs typically move back to the past perfect.
quests.explanation: The present perfect 'has been' shifts to the past perfect 'had been' in reported speech.

quests.partialSentence: My grandfather is ____ old to climb stairs without help now.
quests.hint: Think about a structure meaning 'more than is good or possible,' placed before the adjective.
quests.explanation: 'Too' goes before an adjective to mean 'more than is good,' as in 'too old to climb stairs.'

quests.partialSentence: My little sister isn't tall ____ to reach the top shelf yet.
quests.hint: Think about a structure meaning 'to the necessary degree,' placed after the adjective.
quests.explanation: 'Enough' goes after an adjective to mean 'to the necessary degree': 'tall enough.'

quests.partialSentence: My nephew is ____ young to understand what's happening yet.
quests.hint: Think about a structure showing something is more than is suitable, before the adjective.
quests.explanation: 'Too' is placed before an adjective to mean 'more than is suitable': 'too young.'

quests.partialSentence: This jacket is ____ expensive for my budget right now.
quests.hint: Think about a structure meaning 'more than is acceptable,' placed before the adjective.
quests.explanation: 'Too' goes before an adjective to mean 'more than is acceptable': 'too expensive.'

quests.partialSentence: I don't have ____ money to buy both items today.
quests.hint: Think about a structure meaning 'a sufficient amount,' placed before a noun.
quests.explanation: 'Enough' can go before a noun to mean 'a sufficient amount': 'enough money.'

quests.partialSentence: These shoes aren't comfortable ____ to wear all day.
quests.hint: This structure follows the adjective and means 'sufficiently' for the purpose.
quests.explanation: 'Enough' goes after an adjective to mean 'to the necessary degree': 'comfortable enough.'

quests.partialSentence: I've decided ____ a vegetarian diet starting next month.
quests.hint: After the verb 'decide,' we generally use the infinitive form.
quests.explanation: 'Decide' is followed by the infinitive (to + verb): 'decided to try.'

quests.partialSentence: She stopped ____ meat a few years ago for health reasons.
quests.hint: After the verb 'stop' (meaning to quit a habit), we use the gerund form.
quests.explanation: 'Stop' followed by a gerund means to quit a habit: 'stopped eating' meat.

quests.partialSentence: We agreed ____ a new recipe for the dinner party.
quests.hint: After the verb 'agree,' we generally use the infinitive form.
quests.explanation: 'Agree' is followed by the infinitive (to + verb): 'agreed to try.'

quests.partialSentence: I've decided ____ a new password for all my accounts.
quests.hint: Remember that 'decide' is typically followed by a to-infinitive.
quests.explanation: 'Decide' takes the infinitive form: 'decided to create.'

quests.partialSentence: He stopped ____ that app because it used too much battery.
quests.hint: After 'stop' meaning to quit doing something, we use the gerund form.
quests.explanation: 'Stop' followed by a gerund means to quit doing something: 'stopped using' the app.

quests.partialSentence: They plan ____ the entire system before the end of the month.
quests.hint: After the verb 'plan,' we generally use the infinitive form.
quests.explanation: 'Plan' is typically followed by the infinitive: 'plan to update.'

quests.partialSentence: You look exhausted; you ____ have slept very well last night.
quests.hint: Think about a deduction that something is unlikely to be true, based on evidence.
quests.explanation: 'Can't have' expresses a strong belief that something was not true, based on the evidence of looking tired.

quests.partialSentence: She hasn't eaten all day, so she ____ be starving by now.
quests.hint: Think about a confident deduction based on clear evidence.
quests.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong, logical deduction based on clear evidence.

quests.partialSentence: He answered every question correctly, so he ____ have studied a lot.
quests.hint: Think about a confident deduction based on his performance.
quests.explanation: 'Must have' shows a confident deduction about a past action, based on evidence.

quests.partialSentence: The show sold out in minutes, so it ____ be extremely popular.
quests.hint: Think about a confident deduction based on the evidence of quick ticket sales.
quests.explanation: 'Must' expresses a strong, logical conclusion based on clear evidence.

quests.partialSentence: He says he watched the whole series in one night, but that ____ be true - it's twenty hours long.
quests.hint: Think about a deduction that something is very unlikely to be true.
quests.explanation: 'Can't' expresses strong doubt that something is true, based on logic.

quests.partialSentence: This actor is in every scene, so the role ____ be the lead character.
quests.hint: Think about a confident deduction based on the evidence given.
quests.explanation: 'Must' shows a confident, logical deduction supported by clear evidence.

quests.partialSentence: ____ the bad weather, the event continued as planned.
quests.hint: Think about a linking word followed directly by a noun phrase, not a full clause.
quests.explanation: 'Despite' is followed by a noun or noun phrase, such as 'despite the bad weather.'

quests.partialSentence: ____ I called twice, nobody answered the phone.
quests.hint: Think about a linking word that introduces a full clause showing contrast.
quests.explanation: 'Although' introduces a full clause showing contrast: 'although I called twice.'

quests.partialSentence: The line was very long; ____, we decided to wait anyway.
quests.hint: Think about a linking word used at the start of a new sentence, often after a semicolon.
quests.explanation: 'However' is often used after a semicolon or full stop to show contrast between two sentences.

quests.partialSentence: ____ feeling tired, she finished all her chores before bed.
quests.hint: Think about a linking word followed directly by a noun phrase or gerund, not a full clause.
quests.explanation: 'Despite' can be followed by a gerund phrase, such as 'despite feeling tired.'

quests.partialSentence: ____ I usually wake up early, I overslept this morning.
quests.hint: This connector needs a complete clause after it to express contrast.
quests.explanation: 'Although' introduces a complete clause expressing contrast: 'although I usually wake up early.'

quests.partialSentence: It was raining heavily; ____, we still went for our usual walk.
quests.hint: Think about a linking word used at the start of a new sentence after a semicolon.
quests.explanation: 'However' is commonly placed after a semicolon to introduce a contrasting idea.
